newsitem.title: UK: Politicians to meet N.Irish Loyalists on truce.
newsitem.headline: Politicians to meet N.Irish Loyalists on truce.

text.p: Intensive efforts were under way on Monday to bolster a shaky Protestant guerrilla truce and ease tension threatening peace moves in British-ruled Northern Ireland.
Pro-British "Loyalist" groups, angered by an IRA bomb attack that shattered peace hopes last week, are still observing a two year ceasefire but have refused to say if it will last.

Loyalist politician Gary McMichael, who wants the truce to stay intact, said it was a case of "so far, so good" after a tense weekend had passed without Loyalist retaliation but he warned against over-confidence.
"I don't think we should get too optimistic. I think we are still at a very delicate stage," McMichael told BBC radio.

A delegation from his Ulster Democratic Party (UDP) was due to have a prison meeting on Monday with convicted guerrillas of the banned Ulster Defence Association (UDA) and Ulster Freedom Fighters (UFF) to discuss the truce question.

An Irish Republican Army bomb at British army headquarters south of Belfast on October 7 killed a soldier and fuelled fears that Loyalists might hit back at members of the region's Irish Catholic minority or plant bombs in the Irish capital, Dublin.
UDA and UFF prisoners have said they are no longer backing the province's peace talks process. Their verdict on the future of the truce could be crucial.
Mo Mowlam, the opposition Labour party's spokeswoman on Northern Ireland, will also have a meeting later with Loyalist prisoners in the high security Maze prison.
"She might be able to indicate enough to the prisoners that they feel able again to back the peace process," UDP spokesman David Adams told the BBC.

The Irish Independent newspaper, published in Dublin, reported on Monday that the extremists' umbrella group, the Combined Loyalist Military Command, had agreed to maintain its truce but that further IRA attacks could lead to reprisals.
The paper quoted what it described as a leading loyalist hardliner as saying that another IRA attack would be "one too many".
Parties to the multilateral peace talks were due later on Monday to have fresh discussions aimed at keeping a four-month talks process on track.
Loyalist prisoners say they want evidence that the multi-party talks, bogged down in wrangling since June, can make progress on a peaceful political settlement.
McMichael said the talks "are the only ray of hope that people have".
Sinn Fein, the IRA's political arm, is excluded from the talks because the republican guerrillas refuse to end hostilities.
